title: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome (PRES) and Drug-Induced Hypersensitivity Syndrome (DIHS) following Immunotherapy and BRAF/MEK Inhibition with Continued Response in Metastatic Melanoma
case_prompt: A 68‐year‐old man with BRAF V600E‐positive metastatic melanoma initially received combination nivolumab and ipilimumab. After disease progression during the fourth cycle, he was switched to encorafenib and binimetinib. Three weeks after starting the BRAF/MEK inhibitors, he developed headache, eye pain, blurred vision, and ataxia without seizures. MRI of the brain showed new, symmetric T2 hyperintense signals in the cerebellum bilaterally without mass effect or enhancement; the cerebral hemispheres were uninvolved. Lumbar puncture revealed elevated protein but no white cells and negative cultures. Four days later, he developed fevers, chills, and a diffuse pruritic rash over his back, chest, abdomen, and proximal arms. Laboratory studies at that time showed a creatinine of 3.24 mg/dL (GFR 18 mL/min/1.73 m2), alkaline phosphatase 257 U/L, AST 235 U/L, ALT 103 U/L, and a normal eosinophil count. ANA was negative. A hepatitis panel demonstrated positive hepatitis A IgM and negative hepatitis B and C. A punch biopsy of the rash showed vacuolar alteration at the dermal–epidermal junction with a mid‐ and upper‐dermal perivascular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate containing a few eosinophils and neutrophils.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. PRES was diagnosed based on acute neurologic symptoms and imaging findings of bilateral cerebellar T2 hyperintense signals without mass effect or enhancement — “the patient was assessed to have experienced PRES based on his neurologic symptoms and MRI results.”  
2. DIHS was considered because of the timing and rash biopsy findings, with a RegiSCAR score of 3–4 — “DIHS was considered in the differential diagnosis and could not be ruled out given RegiSCAR grading of 3–4.”  
3. SJS/TEN was excluded due to absence of painful skin, mucosal involvement, characteristic bullae or necrosis, and non‐compatible histopathology — “The rash was not found to be consistent with Stevens-Johnson Syndrome/Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (SJS/TEN) given the lack of painful skin, mucosal involvement, characteristic bullae/superficial necrosis, and discordant histopathologic features.”  
4. Acute hepatitis A was unlikely to be the cause despite positive IgM, as the patient was asymptomatic and exposure timing was unclear — “the patient was clinically asymptomatic despite positive hepatitis A IgM with unclear timing of exposure.”
